title: Lines of best fit
subtitle: Draw a line that follows the pattern, and use it to estimate values.

questions.prompt: What is a line of best fit?
questions.correct: A straight line that follows the pattern, through the middle of the points.
questions.feedback: Yes. About as many points sit above it as below it.

wrong.label: A line that joins every point, dot to dot.
wrong.feedback: A line of best fit is one straight line. It doesn't join the dots.

wrong.label: A line from the first point to the last point.
wrong.feedback: It doesn't have to go through any point. It goes through the middle of them all.

wrong.label: A straight line that must start at 0.
wrong.feedback: It doesn't have to start at 0. It just follows the points.

questions.prompt: Which graph shows the line of best fit?
questions.feedback: Yes. It ignores the outlier and follows the other points.

wrong.label: A
wrong.feedback: That line has been pulled down towards the outlier. Ignore it.

wrong.label: C
wrong.feedback: The points go up, but that line goes down.

wrong.label: D
wrong.feedback: Most points are below that line. It should go through the middle.

questions.prompt: Someone says, "The line of best fit says 3 kWh of heating at 7 °C." Are they right?
questions.correct: No. 3 kWh is a point. The line gives about 4 kWh.
questions.feedback: Yes. Estimates come from the line, not from one point.

wrong.label: Yes. There's a point at 7 °C and 3 kWh.
wrong.feedback: Estimates come from the line, not from one point. The line gives about 4 kWh.

wrong.label: No. The line gives about 7 kWh.
wrong.feedback: 7 is the temperature. Go up to the line, then across to the side axis.

wrong.label: No. You can only estimate where the line goes through a point.
wrong.feedback: You can read the line anywhere. It doesn't need a point there.

questions.prompt: A scatter graph shows revision from 1 to 9 hours. Why can you trust an estimate for 6 hours?
questions.correct: 6 hours is inside the data. There are points either side of it.
questions.feedback: Yes. The points around it show the pattern.

wrong.label: There's a point at exactly 6 hours.
wrong.feedback: You don't need a point there. What matters is that 6 hours is inside the data.

wrong.label: Every estimate from a line of best fit is exact.
wrong.feedback: An estimate is never exact. Inside the data it's reliable.

wrong.label: 6 is in the middle of the bottom axis.
wrong.feedback: Where it sits on the axis doesn't matter. What matters is that it's inside the data.

questions.prompt: A scatter graph shows temperatures from 1 °C to 9 °C. Someone uses the line of best fit to estimate the heating used at 15 °C. Why might this be unreliable?
questions.correct: 15 °C is outside the data. The pattern might not carry on.
questions.feedback: Yes. There are no points out there to show the pattern.

wrong.label: There's no point at 15 °C.
wrong.feedback: Inside the data there's often no point either. The problem is that 15 °C is outside the data.

wrong.label: 15 °C would be an outlier.
wrong.feedback: An outlier is a point that doesn't fit. This is about where the data stops.

wrong.label: The line goes down, so you can't estimate from it.
wrong.feedback: You can estimate from a line that goes down. The problem is that 15 °C is outside the data.

points.text: A line of best fit is a straight line that follows the pattern, through the middle of the points.
About as many points sit above it as below it.
Ignore the outlier when you draw it.
To estimate, go from one axis to the line, then to the other axis. Read the line, not a point.
An estimate inside the data is reliable. Outside the data it may not be, because the pattern might not carry on.
